read.sections.0.text.note: Terms: người sản xuất (producer), người tiêu dùng (consumer): my choices, not in KEY_TERMS. Check that 'hàng hóa' as 'a thing you can touch' reads well, since in Vietnamese 'hàng hóa' usually means 'goods for sale'. | Review: Glossary 'người sản xuất / người tiêu dùng' are standard school terms; check they are clear for slow readers.
read.sections.0.text.source: No person can make everything they use. Think about a simple notebook. One person made the paper, another carried the notebooks to a market and another sold them. The things people exchange are goods and services. A good is a thing you can touch and use, such as rice or a pencil. A service is something useful that a person does for someone else, such as teaching, fixing a bicycle or cutting hair. A producer is a person or group that makes a good or provides a service. A consumer is a person who uses or buys it. At Lakeside Market, Ana is a producer when she sells tomatoes. She is also a consumer when she buys rice.
read.sections.0.text.back: No one can make by themselves everything they use. Think about a simple notebook. One person makes the paper, another person carries the notebooks to the market and another person sells them. The things people exchange are goods and services. Goods are things you can touch and use, like rice or a pencil. Services are useful work that one person does for another, like teaching, repairing a bicycle or cutting hair. A producer is a person or a group who makes goods or provides services. A consumer is a person who uses or buys them. At Lakeside market, Ana is a producer when she sells tomatoes. She is also a consumer when she buys rice.

read.sections.1.heading.note: 'Hàng đổi hàng và tiền': see learningGoal note. | Review: 'hàng đổi hàng' for barter: natural and clear; confirm. Also 'buôn bán' for trade can suggest big commerce; check it suits children swapping at a market.

read.sections.1.text.note: 'Cách này gọi là hàng đổi hàng' defines barter. The standard text keeps 'hàng đổi hàng' for skill swaps (Ravi and Nadia) too; check that reads right. 'giữ giá trị cho về sau' for 'keep value for later'.
read.sections.1.text.source: Sometimes people swap goods or services without using money. This is called barter. At Lakeside Market, Kofi swaps some of his bread for some of Sara's eggs. Ravi fixes Nadia's bicycle, and in return Nadia helps Ravi's sister with reading. Barter still happens in many places today. However, it has a problem: both people must want what the other person has, at the same time. Leo has fish and wants rice, but the rice seller does not want fish. Money solves this problem. Leo can sell his fish and use the money to buy rice. Money also helps people compare prices and keep value for later.
read.sections.1.text.back: Sometimes people swap goods or services with each other without using money. This way is called goods-for-goods swapping (barter). At Lakeside market, Kofi swaps some of his bread for some of Sara's eggs. Ravi repairs a bicycle for Nadia, and in return Nadia helps Ravi's sister learn to read. Today, barter still takes place in many places. However, this way has a problem: both people must want the thing the other has, at the same time. Leo has fish and wants rice, but the rice seller does not want fish. Money solves this problem. Leo can sell the fish and then use the money to buy rice. Money also helps people compare prices and keep value for later.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: I repeated 'Leo' instead of using a pronoun; check for natural flow.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Sometimes people swap things with no money. This is called barter. Kofi gives Sara bread, and she gives him eggs. Ravi fixes a bike, and Nadia helps his sister read. But barter has a problem. Both people must want what the other has. Leo has fish. He wants rice. The rice seller does not want fish. Money helps here. Leo can sell his fish for money. Then he can buy rice.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Sometimes people swap things with each other without using money. This way is called barter. Kofi gives bread to Sara, and Sara gives eggs to Kofi. Ravi repairs a bicycle, and Nadia helps Ravi's sister learn to read. But barter has a problem. Both people must want the thing the other has. Leo has fish. Leo wants rice. The rice seller does not want fish. Money helps here. Leo can sell fish for money. Then Leo buys rice.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Buying and selling relies on trust

read.sections.2.text.note: 'cân đo công bằng' for 'scales are fair' and 'fair weights and measures'. 'Hàng nghìn năm nay' for 'for thousands of years'.
read.sections.2.text.source: Every exchange depends on trust. A buyer trusts that the food is fresh and the scales are fair. A seller trusts that the payment is real. People also trust each other to keep promises, like Nadia's promise to help with reading. If people cheat, others stop trusting them, and trade becomes harder for everyone. This is one reason many markets have rules about fair weights and measures. For thousands of years, markets have brought people together to trade. When people trade fairly, they meet more of their needs, and communities become more connected.
read.sections.2.text.back: Every exchange relies on trust. The buyer trusts that the food is still fresh and the weighing and measuring is fair. The seller trusts that the money paid is real. People also trust each other to keep promises, like Nadia's promise to help learn to read. If someone cheats, others will no longer trust them, and buying and selling becomes harder for everyone. This is one reason many markets have rules on fair weighing and measuring. For thousands of years, markets have brought people together to buy and sell. When people trade fairly, they meet more needs, and communities become more bonded with each other.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: Check it keeps the same ideas as the standard text.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Trade needs trust. A buyer trusts that the food is fresh. A seller trusts that the money is real. People trust each other to keep a promise. If someone cheats, people stop trusting them. Then trade gets harder for everyone. Markets have brought people together for a very long time. When people trade fairly, they get more of what they need.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Buying and selling needs trust. The buyer trusts that the food is still fresh. The seller trusts that the money is real. People trust each other to keep promises. If someone cheats, people no longer trust them. Then buying and selling is harder for everyone. Markets have brought people together for a very long time. When people trade fairly, they get more of the things they need.

write.example.source: In this exchange, Ravi gives Nadia a service. He fixes her bicycle. In return, Ravi's little sister gets help with reading from Nadia for one week. watch.summary.note: Describes a video for younger learners. 'nhu cầu thiết yếu' and 'mong muốn' match Lesson 20. 'Phi công', 'thủ thư' and 'đầu bếp' for pilot, librarian and chef. 'bánh pizza' kept for 'pizza'.
watch.summary.source: This short video for younger learners explains goods and services. First, it reminds you about needs and wants. Needs are things you must have to live, like food, water and a place to live. Wants are things you would like, like toys and games. People use money to get goods and services. Goods are things people make or grow to sell, like food, books and toys. Services are work people do for others. A doctor helps people stay healthy. A pilot flies a plane. A chef cooks food. Then the video gives some puzzles. A book is a good, but a librarian gives a service when they help you find one. A pizza is a good, but bringing it to your home is a service.
watch.summary.back: This short video for younger children explains goods and services. First, the video reminds you about essential needs and wishes. Essential needs are things you must have to live, like food, water and a place to live. Wishes are things you like to have, like toys and games. People use money to get goods and services. Goods are things people make or grow to sell, like food, books and toys. Services are work people do for others. A doctor helps people be healthy. A pilot flies a plane. A chef cooks food. Then the video gives a few riddles. A book is goods, but a librarian does a service when helping you find it. A pizza is goods, but bringing it to your house is a service.
